deep.reconstruction: Context: the previous page is astronomical work dated 1807 (elements of Vesta and solar positions). This page is a number-theoretic draft. It is evidently the core of Gauss's 'third' proof of quadratic reciprocity, published as 'Theorematis arithmetici demonstratio nova' (1808). Notation. Let p be an odd prime, p not dividing k, and m=(p-1)/2. Gauss writes (k/p) for mu(k,p), the number of the products k,2k,...,mk whose least positive residues mod p lie on one side of p/2. Formula 1 shows the intended side is the residues greater than p/2; see errors. [x] is 'the integer next below x', i.e. floor(x) for non-integral x. (1) mu = sum_{j=1}^{m} ([2jk/p] - 2[jk/p]). Reason (mine): [2y]-2[y] = [2{y}], which is 1 if the fractional part {y} > 1/2 and 0 otherwise. With y=jk/p, {jk/p} > 1/2 exactly when the residue of jk exceeds p/2. So this is Gauss's lemma count written with integer parts. (2) [x]+[-x] = -1 for non-integral x. (3) mu(k)+mu(-k) = (p-1)/2. Reason: the residue of -jk is p minus the residue of jk, so exactly one of the two lies above p/2. (4) Rewriting (1) as a sum over j <= m only (implicit steps mine). - The even multipliers 2j that are <= m stay as they are. - The even multipliers 2j > m are written as 2j = p-i, with i odd and i <= m. - Then [(p-i)k/p] = k-1-[ik/p]; this is formula (2) applied to ik/p. - The number of odd i <= m is ceil(m/2), which is (p+1)/4 if p ≡ 3 mod 4 and (p-1)/4 if p ≡ 1 mod 4. This is Gauss's '1/4(p∓1)'. - Hence mu = 1/4(p∓1)(k-1) - 3[k/p] - [2k/p] - 3[3k/p] - ...: coefficient 3 on odd multipliers, 1 on even ones, all multipliers <= m. This is Gauss's first line. - Equivalently: mu = 1/4(p∓1)(k-1) - 2{[k/p]+[3k/p]+[5k/p]+... (odd multipliers <= (p-1)/2)} - {[k/p]+[2k/p]+...+[mk/p]}. Consequence (implicit, mine): for odd k, (k-1)·ceil(m/2) is even. So mu ≡ sum_{j=1}^{m}[jk/p] (mod 2), and Gauss's lemma gives (k|p) = (-1)^{sum [jk/p]}. Side note. The scribbles '[p/k] 0, [2p/k]-[p/k] 1, [3p/k]-[2p/k] 2' are the beginning of the reciprocal count. The number of j with [jk/p]=r is [(r+1)p/k]-[rp/k]. General lemma. Let x be such that no jx and no r/x is an integer, and let h=[nx]. The number of i<=n with [ix]=r is [(r+1)/x]-[r/x], and the top value h occurs n-[h/x] times. So [x]+[2x]+...+[nx] = 0·[1/x] + 1{[2/x]-[1/x]} + 2{[3/x]-[2/x]} + ... + h{n-[h/x]}. Summing by parts gives the boxed identity: [x]+[2x]+...+[nx] + [1/x]+[2/x]+...+[h/x] = nh. Numerical check on the page: x=0.31, n=4. The multiples are 0.31, 0.62, 0.93, 1.24, so the floor sum is 1 and h=1. Also [1/0.31]=3, and 1+3 = 4 = nh. Application (implicit, mine). Take x=k/p with k
errors: The verbal definition says the residues fall 'infra 1/2 p' (below p/2). But formula (1) counts residues ABOVE p/2, as in the published 1808 version. Either 'infra' is a slip for 'supra', or (1) gives (p-1)/2 minus the defined quantity. Formula (3) holds either way.
In (4) the left side is written 'k/p' without the round brackets; it means (k/p)=mu.
The constant must be read as 1/4(p∓1)(k-1), i.e. ceil((p-1)/4)(k-1), depending on p mod 4. Read as 1/4(p-1)(k-1) the formula is wrong for p ≡ 3 mod 4. Example: p=7, k=3 gives 2 instead of mu=1.
The odd-index sum in (4) must stop at the largest odd number <= (p-1)/2. The upper limit written (read as '(p-3)k/p') is ambiguous; if read literally as p-3 it is wrong.
The identity sum[ix] + sum[i/x] = nh tacitly requires that no ix (i<=n) and no r/x (r<=h) be an integer. This holds for x=k/p with p,k distinct primes and n<p, but it is not stated.
Formula (2) holds only for non-integral x. This is fine in the application, since p does not divide jk.
The final '+[h]{n-[h/x]}' should read h·{n-[h/x]}, since h is already an integer.
